items.content: Iranian-backed Houthi militants targeted a tanker in the third such attack on commercial shipping in three days, U.S. Central Command said, as President Biden acknowledged that U.S. strikes have not deterred the Yemen-based group. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he “told our American friends” that he opposes Palestinian statehood after the war, despite the United States emphasizing the importance of a two-state solution.
U.S. personnel were being evaluated for traumatic brain injuries, according to Centcom, which did not respond to a request for comment on whether any U.S. troops were wounded.

items.content: The attack was claimed by the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, a coalition that includes militias backed by Iran. In a statement, the group said the strike was part of the broader resistance against the presence of U.S. troops in Iraq, as well as a response to Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.
Here’s what to know

content: The Houthis’ attempted attack late Thursday on a U.S.-owned tanker followed another round of U.S. strikes targeting Houthi anti-ship missiles. For months, the Houthis have been attacking ships in the Red Sea in what they say is retaliation for Israel’s military campaign in the Gaza Strip. National Security Council spokesman John Kirby said the U.S. strikes will continue for as long as necessary “to disrupt and degrade the Houthis’ ability to continue to conduct these attacks.”

Netanyahu said that under “any future agreement, Israel must have security control over the entire territory from the sea to the Jordan River,” even though it “clashes with the ideas of sovereignty” for Palestinians. Kirby responded that the United States and Israel “obviously see it differently,” noting that “we’re not going to stop working” toward a two-state solution.

A member of Israel’s inner war cabinet criticized Netanyahu’s approach to the war Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief whose son was killed in Gaza, said he did not trust Netanyahu, and he argued that the remaining hostages can only be returned through a deal with Hamas. There have been growing signs of disagreement among political and military leaders over the war and Netanyahu’s leadership.

Mexico and Chile referred the situation in Gaza to the International Criminal Court for investigation over “the latest escalation of violence, particularly against civilian targets, and the alleged continued commission of crimes.” Last week, Israel defended itself at the International Court of Justice against South Africa’s allegations that it is committing genocide in Gaza.

At least 24,762 people have been killed in Gaza and 62,108 wounded since the war began, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Israel estimates that about 1,200 people were killed in Hamas’s Oct. 7 attack.

items.content: Photographers capture rare moments of joy at three weddings in Rafah
By Morgan Coates and Victoria Bisset

authors.name: Morgan Coates
authors.bio: Morgan Coates is the photo editor at The Washington Post’s London hub, playing a key role in the newsroom's global expansion and covering breaking news as it unfolds in the United States and around the globe.

authors.name: Victoria Bisset
authors.bio: Victoria Bisset is a breaking-news reporter for The Washington Post's London Hub, covering the most urgent and consequential stories as they unfold on the European day.

items.content: Rafah, close to the border with Egypt, has become home to massive numbers of people fleeing violence and Israeli airstrikes elsewhere in the besieged enclave. However, photographers have still managed to capture rare moments of joy — including weddings held in camps, tents or abandoned schools in the area.
Afnan Jibril and her partner, Mustafa Shamlakh, gathered with relatives to celebrate their wedding last week, Agence France-Presse reports.
According to the groom’s uncle, the house the couple were supposed to share was destroyed.

“The usual preparations for marriage are not possible, and traditional ceremonies are not feasible,” Mohamed Jibril, the bride’s father, told AFP. “However, clothes are available, although they are scarce and expensive.”
The bride, wearing a traditional-style Palestinian dress and flower crown, joined her groom and guests to dance, as guests sprayed white mousse.
“We are a people that love life, despite death, murders and destruction,” Mohamed Jibril said.

items.content: Public health continues to deteriorate in the Gaza Strip amid intense Israeli bombardment, dwindling resources and poor sanitary conditions. Illness is spreading in crowded shelters, and vulnerable Gazans, including 60,000 who are pregnant, have limited access to medical care, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said in its latest update.

The situation has been compounded by difficulties in getting aid into Gaza. Ted Chaiban, deputy chief of UNICEF, said in a statement Thursday that once aid enters the territory, “our ability to distribute it becomes a matter of life and death.”

Iranian-backed Houthi militants targeted a tanker in the third such attack on commercial shipping in three days, U.S. Central Command said, as President Biden acknowledged that U.S. strikes have not deterred the Yemen-based group. items.content: Paragraph after Gallery is ended

Speaking after a three-day visit to Gaza, Chaiban said he witnessed “some of the most horrific conditions I have ever seen. Since my last visit, the situation has gone from catastrophic to near collapse.”

“UNICEF has described the Gaza Strip as the most dangerous place in the world to be a child. We have said this is a war on children,” he continued. “But these truths do not seem to be getting through.”

The Gaza Health Ministry on Thursday reported more than 8,000 cases of viral hepatitis A linked to overcrowding in shelters, noting that hospital laboratories are unable to conduct blood testing because of a lack of materials. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of the World Health Organization, wrote on social media that 24 cases have been confirmed, while several thousand people have jaundice, “presumably also due to Hepatitis A.”
Testing capacity is “extremely limited,” he added.

Transmitted through contaminated food or water, or through contact with an infectious person, hepatitis A is rarely fatal but can cause “debilitating symptoms,” according to the WHO. Tedros said the “inhumane living conditions” in Gaza will allow the virus to spread and highlight how “explosively dangerous the environment is for the spread of disease.”
Current water and sanitation conditions pose “a high risk for further spread,” OCHA echoed in its update, which also noted that the amount of available water in the territory is “shrinking each day.”

As casualties mount, medical workers and hospitals are also facing danger. The Palestine Red Crescent Society said early Friday that there was “intense artillery shelling” near al-Amal Hospital in Khan Younis. On Thursday, the organization said that since the start of the war, eight colleagues from its ambulance teams have been killed while evacuating the wounded.

A compound housing emergency medical staff from Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) and the International Rescue Committee was “severely damaged as a result of a missile strike,” and a number of team members suffered injuries, MAP said Thursday on social media.

Gaza’s Health Ministry said the health-care infrastructure in Rafah, where many have sought refuge in response to bombardment in the north and central Gaza, is “extremely fragile” and cannot meet the needs of some 1.3 million people there.
Israeli cabinet member lays bare government divisions in frank interview
By Itay Stern and Paul Schemm

items.fullcaption: Israeli cabinet minister and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is consoled by Israeli President Isaac Herzog, as he attends the December funeral of his son, who was killed in northern Gaza during the ongoing ground operation by Israel's military. (Clodagh Kilcoyne/Reuters)
items.blurb: Israeli cabinet minister and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is consoled by Israeli President Isaac Herzog, as he attends the December funeral of his son, who was killed in northern Gaza during the ongoing ground operation by Israel's military.

items.content: TEL AVIV — In a frank interview on Israeli television, a member of the government’s war cabinet slammed the prime minister’s approach to the war in Gaza and urged a deal to release the rest of the hostages held there.

Gadi Eisenkot, a retired general whose own son was killed in the Gaza Strip, told the “Uvda” show, Israel’s equivalent of the CBS program “60 Minutes,” that he did not trust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to tell the truth and that the more than 100 Israeli hostages still in Gaza could be brought back only through a deal with their captors.

items.content: “I think we need to assert that it is impossible to bring back the hostages alive in the near future without going through a deal,” he said. Anyone who tells the public something different “is selling illusions,” he added, referring to Netanyahu’s assertion that the hostages could be freed through a ground war.
The interview, which was recorded earlier, was aired Thursday night and followed a televised speech by Netanyahu in which he reiterated that total victory over Hamas was the only way forward.

The Israeli government has presented two objectives in the war following the Oct. 7 assault by Hamas: to destroy the militant group and bring home the hostages. But Israelis, especially the families of hostages, have expressed growing doubts that the two goals are compatible.
“During the cabinet discussions, I said that if the issue of the hostages is not prioritized, then I am resigning from my position,” Eisenkot said.

He also described how the war cabinet, which includes opposition members like himself, prevented Netanyahu and the heads of the army from launching an attack on the militant Hezbollah group in Lebanon in October, which he said would have realized Hamas’s goal of widening the conflict.
“We prevented a very wrong decision,” he said, describing a shouting match in the cabinet.

Eisenkot was the army chief of staff from 2015 to 2019 and said that he bears responsibility for the cross-border attack by Hamas. He also said that Netanyahu as prime minister also bears clear responsibility for what he called “the worst event in the country’s history.”

Netanyahu formed an emergency unity government with his political rivals shortly after the war began. However, there have been growing signs of disagreement among political and military leaders over the war and Netanyahu’s leadership.
Schemm reported from London.
How Israel’s war in Gaza became a tangled crisis spanning the Middle East
By Adam Taylor

items.fullcaption: Supporters of pro-Iran factions wave various flags in Baghdad's Tahrir Square on Saturday during a protest against U.S. and British forces in Iraq and strikes targeting Yemen's Houthi rebels. (Murtaja Lateef/AFP/Getty Images)
items.blurb: Supporters of pro-Iran factions wave various flags in Baghdad's Tahrir Square on Saturday during a protest against U.S. and British forces in Iraq and strikes targeting Yemen's Houthi rebels. (Murtaja Lateef/AFP/Getty Images)

items.content: Israel’s war in Gaza is at the center of a simmering regional crisis that has threatened to boil over in recent days, which have seen a string of strikes across the Middle East — some direct reverberations of Israel’s effort to root out Hamas.

As Israel targeted Hezbollah sites deep in southern Lebanon and the United States conducted a new round of strikes on what officials said were Houthi missile sites in Yemen, Iran launched strikes at what it said was an Israeli intelligence site in Iraq’s Kurdistan province and a militant site in Pakistan — prompting angry objections from both governments. Iran has also launched strikes into Syria, and its proxy groups in Iran and Syria have targeted U.S. troops there.
As strikes cascade, experts warn that a simple miscalculation could quickly spiral out of control.

“They’re playing a very dangerous game — it’s chicken, basically,” Joost Hiltermann, a Middle East expert at the International Crisis Group, said this month of the various governments and militant groups increasingly enmeshed in regional tensions. “Any miscalculation, any miscommunication, any accidental strike could trigger a major escalation.”

Some suggest that a regional conflict is already underway. Late last month, Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant told a parliamentary committee that the country was defending itself in a “multi-arena” war that went beyond Gaza and the West Bank.
“I say here in the most explicit way: Anyone who acts against us is a potential target. There is no immunity for anyone,” he said.
Here are some of the flash points across the region.

items.blurb: In an evening address to the nation Jan. 18, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the idea of creating a Palestinian state after the war in Gaza.
items.title: Netanyahu says he opposes creation of Palestinian state
items.fullcaption: In an evening address to the nation Jan. 18, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the idea of creating a Palestinian state after the war in Gaza. (Reuters)

items.content: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he told the United States of his opposition to plans for Palestinian statehood in any postwar scenario, arguing that they jeopardize Israeli security — even as U.S. diplomatic efforts to revive the two-state solution continue.

“In any future agreement, Israel must have security control over the entire territory from the sea to the Jordan River,” Netanyahu said in a televised news conference Thursday. “This is a necessary condition, and it clashes with the ideas of sovereignty” for the Palestinians.

“What can we do? I told our American friends this truth, and I will not compromise the attempt to harm Israel’s security. The prime minister of Israel needs to know how to say no, even to our good friends,” he continued.
The United States has continued to offer Israel unwavering support in the war in Gaza, but President Biden has directly called for a two-state solution to the conflict.
Asked about Netanyahu’s position on Thursday, National Security Council spokesman John Kirby responded that the Israeli prime minister’s comments were “not new.”
“We obviously see it differently,” he said. “We believe that the Palestinians have every right to live in an independent state with peace and security.”
Earlier this week, Secretary of State Antony Blinken also said Israel would not be able to achieve “genuine security” without a “pathway” to Palestinian statehood.
“Of course, it requires very difficult, challenging decisions. It requires a mind-set that is open to that perspective,” he said.
U.S. launches new round of strikes against Yemen’s Houthis; Houthis attack another ship
By Karen DeYoung and Sammy Westfall

authors.name: Karen DeYoung
authors.bio: Karen DeYoung is associate editor and senior national security correspondent for The Post. In more than three decades at the paper, she has served as bureau chief in Latin America and in London and as correspondent covering the White House, U.S. foreign policy and the intelligence community.

authors.bio: Sammy Westfall is an assistant editor on The Washington Post's Foreign desk.
authors.expertise: Assistant Editor on the Foreign desk

items.content: The United States fired another round of strikes Thursday morning against Houthi militants in Yemen, targeting “a couple of anti-ship missiles that we had reason to believe were being prepared for imminent fire into the southern Red Sea,” National Security Council spokesman John Kirby said. Later in the day, the Houthis attacked another U.S.-owned ship — the third attack on commercial shipping vessels in three days, the United States said.

The U.S. strikes, which the Pentagon said were carried out by Navy fighter jets, were the second in less than 24 hours. The U.S. Navy on Wednesday night struck 14 missiles it said the Houthis had “loaded to be fired” against merchant vessels and American warships, according to U.S. Central Command.
Kirby said President Biden authorized the strikes as commander in chief under Article II authorities in the Constitution, and under Article 51 of the U.N. charter authorizing self-defense.

Houthi militants have been undeterred by U.S. strikes, continuing to attack commercial vessels. On Thursday night local time in Yemen, Houthi militants launched two anti-ship ballistic missiles at M/V Chem Ranger, a U.S.-owned, Greek-operated, Marshall Island-flagged tanker ship, the U.S. Central Command said in a statement. Though the crew watched the missiles impact nearby water, the ship and its crew were not hurt or damaged, the statement continued.
The Houthis have connected their wave of attacks to the war on Gaza, saying they will continue to launch in protest of Israel’s campaign against Hamas.
Dan Lamothe and Alex Horton contributed to this report.

Stock traders earned millions of dollars anticipating the Hamas attack, a study found.
